readerTitle: Why your first salesperson should be you
caseNote: 가상 사례 (병원 대상 기장 서비스, 동네 식당의 단체 행사) + 실무자 관찰 (Steve Blank, Paul Graham)
insight: 초기 영업은 매출을 만드는 일이기 전에 고객이 무엇을 사는지 배우는 조사이고, 그 지식은 아직 없기 때문에 남에게 맡길 수 없다.
misconception: 창업자는 만드는 사람이고, 영업은 경험 많은 영업 담당자를 빨리 뽑아 맡기면 된다.

sources.text: Graham, P. (2013). Do Things That Don't Scale. paulgraham.com
Blank, S. (2005). The Four Steps to the Epiphany (customer development, "get out of the building")
Maya와 식당 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Paul Graham의 'Do Things That Don't Scale'(2013년 7월) 에세이가 창업자가 초기 사용자를 직접 하나씩 모아야 한다고 주장하는지 원문으로 다시 확인하세요.
'Get out of the building'이 Steve Blank의 고객 개발(customer development) 방법론에서 쓰는 표현이라는 점과 책 출간 연도(2005)를 확인하세요.
Maya의 통화 수(15건), 통화 시간(40분 중 5분 발언), 세 가지 패턴은 모두 설명용 가상 내용입니다. 실제 통계처럼 읽히지 않는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: The founder who talked for five minutes
body: Maya runs a new bookkeeping service for small medical clinics. Her first sales call lasted 40 minutes. She spoke for about five.
The clinic manager barely mentioned bookkeeping. She kept coming back to insurance payments that arrive months late. That one complaint turned out to be worth more than any sales script.

image.label: A founder listening on a call, taking notes
image.brief: 작은 사무실 책상에서 창업자가 전화를 들고 고개를 끄덕이며 노트에 메모하는 장면. 노트에는 "late insurance payments"에 밑줄. 상대방 쪽 말풍선이 크고 창업자 쪽 말풍선은 작게. 실제 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: Who should win the first clients?
body: Maya is a great bookkeeper and a nervous seller. Her service is ready, and she has savings for one hire.
How should she find her first clients?

options.text: Hire an experienced salesperson on commission
options.feedback: She frees her own time, but the salesperson has nothing proven to sell yet. Every lesson from those calls stays in someone else's head.

options.text: Make the first sales calls herself, nerves and all
options.feedback: It costs her time and comfort. In return she hears exactly why clinics say yes or no, and she can change the offer on the spot.

options.text: Spend the money on ads and a better website
options.feedback: Ads can bring in leads. But clicks don't tell her what clinics really struggle with, so she'd still be guessing what to say.

cards.title: What the first 15 calls taught her
body: Maya kept making the calls herself. By the fifteenth, three patterns were clear.
list: The real pain was **chasing late insurance payments**, not monthly books
The person who decides is the office manager, not the doctor
Clinics trust a word from another clinic more than any ad
cards.callout: She rebuilt her offer around late payments. Her pitch got shorter, and clinics said yes faster.

cards.title: Founder-led selling
body: **Founder-led selling** means the founder personally makes the early sales, before anyone is hired to sell.

Early sales aren't only about revenue. They are the fastest way to learn what customers actually want, what they will pay for, and what makes them hesitate. That knowledge doesn't exist yet, so nobody else can be trained in it.

image.label: A founder turning call notes into a playbook
image.brief: 왼쪽에 흩어진 통화 메모 카드들, 가운데 창업자가 이를 정리하는 모습, 오른쪽에 깔끔하게 묶인 "Playbook" 책자. 왼쪽에서 오른쪽으로 흐르는 화살표. 플랫 일러스트, 로고 없음.

cards.title: Three things only the founder can do
body: In the first deals, the founder has advantages no new hire has.
list: **Hear the real problem**, and know which complaints matter for the offer
**Change the offer on the spot**: price, scope, even the product itself
**Earn trust**: early customers are betting on a person, not a track record
cards.callout: A salesperson runs a playbook. The founder's early sales write it.

cards.title: Experienced founders keep giving the same advice.
body: Steve Blank, who shaped the customer development method, tells founders to "get out of the building" and talk to customers themselves. Paul Graham's 2013 essay "Do Things That Don't Scale" argues that founders should recruit their early users by hand.
In both views, early selling is research that happens to pay.
cards.softwareNote: Software founders often hope a launch page or ads will replace sales calls. Sign-ups show who clicked, not why they stayed or left. The founder hears those reasons in the first demos and onboarding calls.

cards.title: Founder selling is a phase, not a job for life.
body: It costs the founder's time, which the business also needs elsewhere. And customers may be buying *you*: your energy and your promises. That can hide whether the offer works without you.
Hand off when you can predict the common objections, the same pitch keeps working, and you can write down what a good deal looks like. Then a hire has something real to follow.

cards.title: Now it's a restaurant.
body: You own a busy neighborhood restaurant and want to start hosting private events in the back room. You're in the kitchen most nights, and inquiries are starting to arrive.

options.text: Give your host a price sheet and let them answer inquiries
options.feedback: Quick and cheap. But the host will answer questions, not learn why guests book or walk away, so you won't know what to change.

options.text: Take the first dozen inquiries yourself, then write a guide for the host
options.feedback: It costs some evenings out of the kitchen. You learn what events people want and what worries them, and the host gets a real playbook.

options.text: Hire an events manager now to grow bookings fast
options.feedback: A good hire needs to know what sells. Right now nobody knows, so you'd be paying a salary to guess.

cards.softwareNote: The same holds for a new app feature for businesses: the founder should run the first customer calls before handing them to a sales or support team.

cards.title: Sell first, so you know what you're selling.
body: Early sales are research that pays. Do them yourself until the pattern is clear, then hand over the playbook.
**Try it today:** write down the last three reasons a customer said yes or no to you. If you can't, you're too far from the sale.
